I assumed PostgreSQL and a `users` table with an `id` primary key, since there is no project here to match; I have not run this against a database.

```sql
-- migrations/20261008_split_full_name.sql
BEGIN;

ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS first_name text,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_name  text;

-- Backfill only rows that have not been split yet, so a second run
-- is a no-op and never overwrites names edited after the first run.
UPDATE users u
SET first_name = split_part(n.name, ' ', 1),
    last_name  = CASE
                   WHEN strpos(n.name, ' ') > 0
                   THEN substr(n.name, strpos(n.name, ' ') + 1)
                 END
FROM (
  SELECT id,
         btrim(regexp_replace(full_name, '\s+', ' ', 'g')) AS name
  FROM users
  WHERE full_name IS NOT NULL
    AND first_name IS NULL
    AND last_name IS NULL
) n
WHERE u.id = n.id
  AND n.name <> '';

COMMIT;
```

- **Running it twice:** `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` skips existing columns, and the backfill only touches rows where both new columns are still `NULL`. The whole thing is in one transaction, so a failed run leaves nothing half-done.
- **Split rule:** the first word becomes `first_name` and everything after it becomes `last_name`, after trimming and collapsing whitespace. "Mary Ann Smith" becomes `Mary` / `Ann Smith`, and a single-word name like "Cher" gets a `NULL` last name. No rule gets every name right, so spot-check the results.
- **`full_name` is kept:** dropping it belongs in a later migration, once the application reads and writes the new columns. Until then, new rows written with only `full_name` can be picked up by re-running this.
- **Large tables:** the single `UPDATE` locks every row it touches until commit. For a table with millions of rows, run the backfill in batches by `id` range outside the transaction instead.

If you use a different database or a migration framework (Alembic, Rails, Knex, Django), tell me which and I'll rewrite it in that form.
